desc:
An initially empty collection of integers receives the values of nums one at a time, from left to right. Inserting a value that is already in the collection changes nothing.

After each insertion, look at the collection as a set and find the longest run of consecutive integers x, x+1, ..., x+L-1 all contained in it. Return an array res of the same length as nums where res[i] is that longest length after inserting nums[i].

For example, nums = [5, 2, 4, 3, 3, 9] gives [1, 1, 1, 4, 4, 4]: after 5 and 2 the best run has length 1, inserting 4 makes the run 4, 5 (length 2), and inserting 3 joins everything into 2, 3, 4, 5 (length 4).

Recomputing the answer from scratch after each insertion is too slow; aim for O(n) overall.
hints: Re-running the longest-consecutive-sequence scan after every insertion costs O(n<sup>2</sup>). The answer should be updated incrementally instead.
A new value x can only merge the run ending at x - 1 with the run starting at x + 1. The new run has length left + 1 + right.

Store the run length in a map only at the two ends of each run. When inserting a new x, read left = len[x-1] and right = len[x+1], then write the combined length at x - left and x + right (and at x itself to mark it as seen). Keep a running maximum.
editorial: The key observation: when x is new, its neighbour x - 1 (if present) is automatically the right end of its run, because x was not there to extend it. Likewise x + 1 is the left end of its run. Maintaining a hash map from run endpoints to run length therefore gives both neighbouring lengths in O(1).

On a new value, compute total = left + right + 1, store it at the new left end x - left and the new right end x + right, and mark x as present (its stored value may become stale if it is an interior point, but interior entries are never read as neighbours of a new value). Update the global maximum and append it to the output. Repeated values are skipped by a membership test. Total time O(n) and space O(n). A union-find over values achieves the same bound.
